messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
Those few lines complicate Majeed’s usual portrait. The cunning is only indirect; the apathy is interrupted. He does not merely stand aside: he wakes Bibi, chooses the village, and physically carries Jamila while Rahima follows. The blinding moonlight adds urgency and even vulnerability. Thus the same traits are present only in shadow: he may still be calculating, and his tone is practical, but he is not openly apathetic here.

I read the action as mostly teleological. Majeed’s rescue is a means to a larger end: moving the women away, protecting the household’s stability, avoiding danger or exposure, and retaining control. A purely deontological act of good-will would be driven by duty for its own sake: he would save them simply because they are in need. Here, the duty-like gesture is embedded in a practical strategy. He saves them, but the saving serves a purpose. There is still a small warmth—the wrapped Jamila and the inclusion of Rahima—so the act is not coldly mechanical, but it is not purely selfless. It is calculated care: a teleological choice with a thin deontological edge.

Palindromic words included: radar, level, civic, rotor, kayak, refer, stats, tenet, madam, deified, reviver, rotator.
